title: 3-Read Friday #83: Effective Prison Work, Multimedia Learning, and the Hidden Lives of Teachers
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #83 pairs an unusual leadership pick with two teacher-focused pieces. Harry Fletcher-Wood shares principles of effective prison work -- communication, conflict management, and behaviour change -- that Barton leaves readers to map onto classroom management. Carl Hendrick digs into a new meta-analysis of Richard Mayer's multimedia learning principles, identifying which design strategies reliably improve learning and under what boundary conditions. Adam Robbins extends Graham Nuttall's "hidden lives of learners" framework by adding a fourth hidden world: the teacher's own beliefs, values, and internal narratives, and what that means for how CPD should be designed. Barton's own week is marked by the launch of his new Tips for Teachers book series, beginning with Cold Call.
points: Fletcher-Wood's prison-work principles -- procedural justice, treating every moment as a rehabilitative opportunity, warmth balanced with boundaries, and consistent use of discretion -- are offered by Barton as a deliberately unusual lens on classroom management.

Hendrick's pick distills a meta-analysis of three decades of Mayer's multimedia research, separating design principles that reliably help learning (text plus diagrams, cutting seductive details) from those that disappoint despite hype (VR).

Robbins' fourth hidden world -- teachers' own beliefs, values, and internal narratives -- reframes CPD design: the same feedback or training can land as encouragement for one teacher and as criticism for another depending on that hidden layer.
Barton frames the issue around his new 16-part Tips for Teachers book series launching with Cold Call, tying the newsletter's practice-focused picks to his own publishing project.
quotes: Something different from Harry - a deep dive into effective prison work: practical ways to communicate effectively, manage conflict, and promote change. I will leave you to decide how many transfer to the classroom.
Carl takes a customery deep dive into a new meta-analysis of Richard Meyer’s multimedia principles.
Carl picks out the principles of design that are likely to have the most impact on student learning, and identifies the boundary conditions that can make or break them.

Graham Nuttall's book, The Hidden Lives of Learners, had a massive impact on my teaching. Nuttall identifies three hidden worlds within our classrooms: the teacher's world, the peer world, and the private world.
In this post, Adam adds a fourth world: the teacher's world of beliefs, values and internal narratives.
